content: Rainwater runs from the roof into the ______.

passageTitle: Section 2 — Rainwater harvesting system
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Green Energy Centre. Before we look at the exhibition, I would like to explain the diagram on the wall behind me. It shows how a rainwater harvesting system works in a normal family house. First, when it rains, the water falls onto the roof of the house. From the roof, it runs down into the gutter, the long metal channel along the edge of the roof. The gutter carries the water to a pipe at the corner of the house. Next, the water passes through a filter, which removes leaves and dirt. Clean water then flows into a large storage tank under the garden. The tank can hold two thousand litres. Finally, when the family needs water for the garden, a small electric pump moves the water from the tank to a tap near the back door. The system is simple and cheap, and it can save a family a large amount of drinking water every year. Now, please follow me to the garden, where you can see a real system at work.

passageTitle: Section 4 — How glass bottles are recycled
script: Good afternoon. In today's lecture, I would like to describe how glass bottles are recycled. The process has several stages. First, used bottles are collected from homes and recycling points and taken to a recycling centre. At the centre, workers sort the bottles by colour: green, brown and clear glass are kept separate, because the colours must not be mixed. Next, the sorted glass is crushed into very small pieces. These pieces are called cullet. The cullet is then washed and heated in a large furnace. Inside the furnace, the temperature is so high that the glass melts and becomes a thick liquid. After that, the liquid glass is poured into moulds and shaped into new bottles. Finally, the new bottles are cooled, checked for cracks, filled with drinks and sent to the shops. In this way, a bottle you throw away today could return to a shop shelf as a new bottle within a few weeks.

passageText:
The bicycle has changed a great deal since it first appeared. The earliest bicycle, known as the draisine, was built in Germany in 1817. It had two wheels and a wooden frame, but it had no pedals. Riders sat on a small seat and pushed the machine along the road with their feet, so it was slow and tiring to use.

In the 1870s, the penny-farthing appeared in Britain. It had a very large front wheel, sometimes more than 1.5 metres high, and a much smaller back wheel. The rider sat high above the ground, which gave a good view of the road, but it was difficult to climb onto the bicycle, and a fall from that height could cause a serious injury.

The next important step came in 1885, when the safety bicycle was built in England. It had two wheels of the same size, a chain to drive the back wheel, and a low frame that was easy to step over. It was also much cheaper to make than the penny-farthing, so ordinary working people could finally afford one. Within a few years, the safety bicycle had become the most popular form of transport in towns and cities, and its basic design is still used today.

content: Which TWO health benefits of gardening does the passage mention? Choose TWO letters, A–G.
explanation: Bài đọc nói làm vườn cho con người không khí trong lành, vận động nhẹ nhàng và giúp quên đi căng thẳng của ngày làm việc.
passageText: In many towns and cities, more and more people are taking up gardening, and researchers have asked why this old activity is becoming popular again. The answers are surprisingly varied. For many people, the first reason is health. Working in a garden gives them fresh air and gentle exercise, and it helps them to forget the stress of the working day. Doctors have found that people who garden regularly often sleep better and feel calmer. A second reason is money. Growing your own vegetables and herbs can save a family a large amount of money over a year, especially when food prices are rising. People also say that home-grown food simply tastes better than food bought in a supermarket. Gardening also brings people together. In community gardens, neighbours meet, share tools and exchange advice, and many new friendships begin over a garden fence. Finally, gardening helps people to learn about nature. They watch the seasons change, learn the names of plants and insects, and understand how soil, water and sunlight work together. For children, a garden can be a first science lesson. Only a small number of gardeners say that they garden in order to win prizes or enter competitions; for most people, the garden is a place to relax, not to compete.
passageTitle: Passage 2 — Why do people take up gardening?

passageText: After years of decline, night trains are returning to Europe's railways. In the 1990s and 2000s, many overnight services were closed because they were expensive to run and because cheap flights took their passengers away. Travellers preferred to fly for one hour rather than spend a whole night on a train. Now the situation is changing. Concern about climate change has made many people look for alternatives to flying, and a night train offers a simple answer: passengers board in the evening, sleep in a comfortable bed, and arrive in another city the next morning, without losing a day to travel. Railway companies have noticed the change. Austria's state railway, for example, has expanded its Nightjet network, and new services now link cities such as Vienna, Paris, Amsterdam and Berlin. Tickets often sell out weeks in advance, especially in summer. The trains are not perfect. They are slower than planes, they can be expensive at busy times, and there are still too few routes. Yet their return shows that many travellers are willing to trade speed for comfort and for a smaller effect on the environment.

options.content: How to Improve Your Memory in One Week
options.label: B

passageText: Most people have had the embarrassing experience of meeting someone they know well and suddenly being unable to remember that person's name. Scientists who study memory say that this is normal, and that it happens for a simple reason. Names are difficult for the brain to store because they are arbitrary: there is no clear link between a person's face and the sound of their name. We remember faces easily because a face has many details to hold on to — eyes, hair, voice and smile. A name, by contrast, is just a sound with no meaning of its own. Forgetting a name is also more common when we are tired, stressed or distracted, because the brain needs attention to bring a stored name back into consciousness. Researchers suggest a few ways to improve. Repeating a name soon after hearing it, using it in conversation, and connecting it to something familiar — for example, picturing a person called Rose holding a rose — can all help the name to stay in memory. However, scientists also note that forgetting names does not usually mean that memory is failing; it is simply how human memory works.
passageTitle: Passage 4 — Why do we forget names?

options.content: The Life of a Queen Bee

passageText: On the roofs of offices, schools and apartment blocks in London, Paris and New York, thousands of bees are now at work. Urban beekeeping — keeping beehives in cities — has grown quickly in the past ten years. City bees often do better than country bees, scientists say, because cities have a surprising variety of flowers: gardens, parks, balconies and even trees along streets flower at different times of the year, giving bees food for a longer season. Cities also use fewer farm chemicals, which can harm bees. For the people who keep them, city hives provide honey and a close connection with nature in the middle of busy streets. Some companies keep hives on their roofs as a way of showing that they care about the environment, and some schools use them to teach children about insects and food. There are difficulties, too. A hive needs a careful keeper, neighbours may worry about stings, and a city can only support a limited number of hives. Yet supporters argue that urban beekeeping has already done something valuable: it has made city people notice, and care about, the small insects on which much of our food depends.
